spiritual_reading:
The Divine teaches that when zeal for what is good rises, it may be turned into a just ordering of what is disorderly. Then whatever resists good is immediately weakened and brought into a state where it must accept the rule of what is true, under a judgment that is genuinely just.

The teaching continues: the zeal you are permitted to have is not the delight of injuring, but a just discernment that labors for amendment. Toward those who are hard to lead, it presses them toward a change of mind. In such cases the severity that appears in zeal is chiefly a warning and a restraint, because it is not meant to destroy but to arrest what is evil. The severity itself is the warning; and when the time requires, you may reprove and correct a companion with words that strike fear, not to disgrace him for its own sake but to bring him into a useful shame, so that the stubborn resistance in him may be removed and his inner intention may be opened to what is right.

Yet another kind of zeal is described, and you are cautioned against it. There is a zeal that is merely a permission for evil desire to find a reason to act, and thus to join itself with sin. One listens only to what supports oneself, and then burns with a heat that comes from self. One fixes the mind on another in order to overpower, and the impulse becomes violent. Nothing is spoken that builds up; instead the mind gathers itself into a cold calculation while the will rages from arrogance and self-display. Such people defame because they want the other to be thought worthless. They refuse to acknowledge what is good in another, and while they burn they pour out abuse and condemnation, craving to cast down those who are gentle, repaying harm with harm and making retaliation into a principle. From this come further evils: either they incite others into doing what is wrong, or, if someone weakens and falls into sin, they use it as an occasion for further condemnation and refuse every just assessment. They withdraw into their own self-rule and will not be aligned with the common understanding of companions. When corrected, they seize upon that correction as a cause for rage and then do what is evil from that rage. This is the zeal that is evil, though it pretends to be zeal, and people still call it zeal.

The teaching therefore distinguishes between destructive rage and healing severity. When you must confront evil or stubborn falsity and someone hardens and will not receive what you offer, you may perceive that he lowers himself into obstinacy. You also recognize that he attributes harshness to you and therefore returns harshness from his own evil. Then you may answer with firm and weighty truth, with a sternness that restrains, not with cruelty but with the strength required to break the delight of resisting. This kind of severity is not truly rage, even if it is felt as painful; it is a strong correction that aims at a change of mind.

For one who corrects rightly is like an understanding healer whose perception is delicate and exact. The disorders to be cured may be severe; therefore the means applied are varied according to the condition. Sometimes what is needed is an ardent influx that searches and stings, sometimes a gentle influx that soothes and binds, and this according to the quality of the injury and according to what has preceded.

Thus some people, if they are met with sharp correction, accept it and are turned; in them the strong truth that strikes is joined with what heals and brings them back into order. Others, if they are met with sharpness, are driven further into resistance; these must be met with a humbling gentleness, and through it they are restored. The truly wise person therefore acts from understanding, adapting speech to the state of the one being corrected. He brings down the proud by truths fitted to their error until they can acknowledge what is right in humility. He also takes care that his correction proceeds from what is godly in him, so that his intention remains pure. He regards a companion in two modes: one mode by which he seeks to lead through what is loving, and another mode by which he restrains through what is fearful. For when the stubborn resistance in someone arises from foolish confidence and from delight in doing evil, that person can sometimes be reached only by a fear that arrests. This fear is not the goal; it is a means that can lead to a change of mind. Yet even then the corrector remains in order within himself, weighing words and their effect, and he continues to press the matter until amendment is produced.

For the enlighteners in the higher heavens appear in these two modes: in the mode of love and in the mode of fear. They show both modes of the higher powers, because their interior life flows through the whole of their being and expresses itself in a complete form. In these two appearances—the mode of love, which is perceived as beauty and elevation, and the mode of opposing presence, which is perceived as confronting and restraining—they cleanse and set in order the higher powers within those who receive them.

fills.notes: The spiritual sense requires an act of setting the resistant state in order under zeal for good: bringing the person into a compelled stance before what judges truly. Hence an ordering verb (make stand, set before) rather than harming.
The place described is where resistance must accept true ordering; in this register it is the place of assessment, not punishment for its own sake.
Opens an impersonal exposition about the permitted kind of zeal, matching the didactic substrate style.
Sets up a definition of the just kind of anger as an instrument of righteous ordering.
Spiritual context: zeal is allowed when it functions as correction and ordering, not injury; therefore it is ‘making in it a judgement of righteousness’ by reproving.
The object is ‘difficult people’ (hard to lead); the phrase needs a preposition introducing them.

fills.fill: so that they may come to
fills.notes: Spiritual sense: severity aims at amendment, i.e., change of mind; thus it presses toward repentance.
Refers back to ‘their anger and wickedness and evil-doing’: the hostile heat is within them, not in the corrector.

fills.fill: it is not to destroy them.
fills.notes: Correspondential constraint: the permitted severity is a restraint and warning, not a will to ruin; this explicit negation stabilizes the distinction.
The text contrasts constant function (anger as scare) with variable application (‘when … you would censure’).
‘Obduracy … in this … his heart’: the gap must carry the indwelling location of resistance, i.e., ‘that is in his heart’.
Introduces the opposite-sense anger (destructive zeal) as a second species, matching the spiritual translation.
Marks the turn from the just zeal to the evil zeal and prepares the defining clause.
The line is a caution: you have heard, but are not to embrace this anger; imperative fits the substrate’s instructional tone.
Spiritual sense: one listens only to what serves self; the gap introduces the condition of refusal to hear what is true.
Completes the idea: selective listening that supports self-will, as in the spiritual translation.
The anger described is from self, not zeal for good—arrogant heat.
‘Look at him … and he is violent’: the gaze is for domination, not discernment.
Opposes abusive speech; in the oldest layer the contrast is between building and tearing down—peace-making, constructive words.
They speak ill so that others will ‘think little of’ the targeted brother; ‘underestimate’ matches the spiritual sense of making him worthless in others’ eyes.
From such rage come further evils: it either incites others into wrongdoing or uses another’s fall as fuel; ‘stir up’ fits the causative function.
The faltering of another is made an occasion ‘because of him’ (on his account) for further accusation.
‘He walks in his own … not of the opinion of his brothers’: ‘mind’ gives the interior self-rule contrasted with common understanding.
Summarizes the evil species: anger joined to zeal in appearance but actually hatred; corresponds to ‘evil zeal’ in the spiritual translation.
Transitions from the description of evil anger to the rule for firm correction, matching the doctrinal, impersonal mode.
Spiritual sense explicitly includes ‘stubborn falsity’ alongside evil; the oldest layer often pairs moral evil with falsity as its form.
The phrase ‘two or one … becomes obdurate’ needs a general noun for the issues produced—evil or false matters.
He ‘becomes obdurate and not listen to you’: the object is the offered correction, i.e., your words.
Spiritual translation: he ‘lowers himself into obstinacy’; this fill matches that motion in the inner sense.
Names the state he assumes ‘up to now’: an interior hardening rather than a temporary mood.
‘You understand that they … harshness to you’: they ascribe it; ‘attribute’ is demanded by the spiritual sense.
A doctor’s hand is ‘sensitive in touching’: the correspondential point is delicate perception of states.
Joins two clauses: severe wounds and varied applications; small connective required.
Introduces the alternation of hot and cool remedies as a rule of application.
Correspondence: varied influx according to condition of the disorder; ‘state’ is the governing idea.
Links the simile back to the preceding description; ‘corresponding to the simile …’ needs ‘that has been said’.

fills.fill: in those who are being corrected.
fills.notes: Completes the generalization: ‘this too is how it happens’—in the recipients of rebuke/correction.
Carries forward the medical correspondence: hard word corresponds to the painful remedy.

fills.fill: So also there are two kinds
fills.notes: The paragraph turns to two recipient types; the fill must introduce the bifurcation.
First type: accepts sharp rebuke and is restored—healing outcome.
Sets the contrast: those harmed by sharpness need gentleness.
Matches ‘driven further into resistance’ in spiritual translation; the opposite of being healed by sharpness.
‘just as this … healed’: needs subject marker for the comparison in the natural text.
Ties the correspondence: cool remedy parallels humbling gentleness.
Connective to continue description of the wise corrector’s action.
He ‘speaks to him … corresponding to error’: the instrument is fitted words or truths.
Captures the end: pressing the proud down by truths until acknowledgment and humility occur.

fills.fill: from what is pure in him,
fills.notes: Spiritual translation: ensure correction proceeds from what is godly so intention remains pure; ‘pure in him’ keeps oldest-layer register without devotional framing.
Completes the purpose clause: keeping the inner end in order.
‘And … so that he might … the brother’: needs an infinitive construction ‘be in’ leading into ‘two aspects’.
He is to ‘regard the brother in two aspects’: dual-mode correction (love, fear).
Pairs with ‘but the other one’: grammatical necessity.
Fear here is not terror for its own sake but restraining confrontation; this term matches the two-aspect doctrine and ¶9’s ‘confrontation’.
Introduces the condition: obduracy present in a brother.
Links ‘foolishness’ with its source (foolish confidence, delight).
What is spoken ‘with great fear’ is firm truth that arrests; this matches the correspondential role of fear as restraint.
Again enforces the substrate distinction: fear is instrumental for repentance, not annihilation.
‘Yet, this one … as even he is … he reckons words’: even when using fear, the corrector must remain ordered within himself; this matches the spiritual translation’s weighing of words and effects.

assessment: Most gaps can be restored at the level of semantic function because the chapter is built on a tight correspondence: two kinds of ‘anger’ (zeal as just correction vs rage from self), and the medical simile (hot and cool remedies) mapping to sharp and gentle speech. Exact Coptic idiom cannot be recovered from the English core alone, so several fills remain moderate, aimed at preserving the oldest, impersonal cosmological-instruction register and the discrete two-aspect structure (love and restraining fear).
